{{Short description|Statistical methods for comparing samples}}
The '''two-proportion Z-test''' (also called the '''two-sample proportion Z-test''') is a [[statistical hypothesis test]] for assessing whether two groups differ in the proportion of a [[Binary data#Binary variable|binary]] outcome, in such a significant way that is beyond chance. For example, the proportion of patients responding positively to a treatment in a [[clinical trial]] versus control, the defect rate in [[quality control]] for two production lines, or the [[click-through rate]] in an [[A/B testing|A/B test]] of two alternative webpage designs.

The test is appropriate when each observation is [[i.i.d|independent]] from another, can be classified as a success or failure (i.e., a [[Bernoulli distribution|Bernoulli]] trial) and the sample sizes are large enough that the sampling distribution of each sample proportion is well approximated by the [[central limit theorem]]. Under those conditions the observed difference of sample proportions can be converted to a standardized [[z-test|z-statistic]] (using a pooled [[standard error]]) and compared to the [[standard normal distribution]] to obtain [[p-value]]s or form [[confidence interval]]s for the difference in proportions (derived slightly differently). This also allows to determine required sample-size for a minimum-detectable-effect calculations.

The test is related to other well known tests such as [[Pearson's chi-squared test]], [[Fisher's exact test]] for small samples, and [[McNemar's test]] for paired binary data.

== Definition ==
The '''two-proportion Z-test''' or '''two-sample proportion Z-test''' is a [[statistical method]] used to determine whether the difference between the proportions of two groups, coming from a [[binomial distribution]] is statistically significant.<ref>[https://stattrek.com/hypothesis-test/difference-in-proportions Hypothesis Test: Difference Between Proportions]</ref> This approach relies on the observation that (for a sufficiently large samples) the sample proportions follow a [[normal distribution]] under the [[Central Limit Theorem]], allowing the construction of a [[z-test]] for [[hypothesis testing]] (a [[Score test]]) and [[confidence interval]] estimation (a [[Wald test]]).<ref name="Su2024">{{cite web |last=Su |first=Wanhua |title=Introduction to Applied Statistics (10.6 Inferences for Two Population Proportions)|url=https://openbooks.macewan.ca/introstats/chapter/10-6-inferences-for-two-population-proportions/
 |publisher=MacEwan University Open Textbooks |year=2024}}</ref> It is used in various fields to compare success rates, response rates, or other proportions across different groups.

== Hypothesis test ==
The [[z-test]] for comparing two proportions is a frequentist [[statistical hypothesis test]] used to evaluate whether two independent samples have different population proportions for a binary outcome. Under mild regularity conditions (sufficiently large sample sizes and independent sampling), the [[Binomial distribution#Estimation of parameters|sample proportions]] (which is the average of observations coming from a [[Bernoulli distribution]]) are [[Asymptotic distribution|approximately]] [[normal distribution|normally distributed]] under the [[Central Limit Theorem|central limit theorem]], which permits using a z-statistic constructed from the difference of sample proportions and an estimated standard error.<ref name="Su2024" />

The test involves two competing hypotheses:
* null hypothesis (H<sub>0</sub>): The proportions in the two populations are equal, i.e., <math>p_1 = p_2</math>.
* alternative hypothesis (H<sub>1</sub>): The proportions in the two populations are not equal, i.e., <math>p_1 \neq p_2</math> ([[One- and two-tailed tests|two-tailed]]) or <math>p_1 > p_2</math> / <math>p_1 < p_2</math> (one-tailed).

The z-statistic for comparing two proportions is computed using:<ref>{{cite book |title=Introductory Statistics 2e |chapter=§10.3 Comparing Two Independent Population Proportions |chapter-url=https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/10-3-comparing-two-independent-population-proportions
 |publisher=OpenStax |year=2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Guthrie |first1=William F. |chapter=§7.3.3 How can we determine whether two processes produce the same proportion of defectives? |chapter-url=https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section3/prc33.htm |title=e-Handbook of Statistical Methods |publisher=NIST/SEMATECH |date=2012 |doi=10.18434/M32189 |url=https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/index.htm}}</ref><ref name ="Kiernan2014">{{cite book |last=Kiernan |first=D. |title=Natural Resources Biometrics |chapter=4. Inferences about the Differences of Two Populations — Section 4 |chapter-url=https://milnepublishing.geneseo.edu/natural-resources-biometrics/chapter/kiernan-chapter-4/|publisher=Milne Publishing (SUNY Geneseo) |year=2014}}</ref><ref name="Su2024" />{{rp|10.6.2}}<math display="block">z = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2}{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}},</math>where <math>\hat{p}_1</math> and <math>\hat{p}_2</math> are the sample proportion in the first and second sample, <math>n_1</math> and <math>n_2</math> are the size of the first and second sample, respectively, <math>\hat{p}</math> is pooled proportion, calculated as <math>\hat{p} = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{n_1 + n_2}</math>, where <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math> are the counts of successes in the two samples The '''pooled proportion''' is used to estimate the shared probability of success under the null hypothesis, and the standard error accounts for variability across the two samples.

The z-test determines statistical significance by comparing the calculated z-statistic to a critical value. E.g., for a significance level of <math>\alpha = 0.05</math> we reject the null hypothesis if <math>|z| > 1.96</math> (for a [[One- and two-tailed tests|two-tailed test]]). Or, alternatively, by computing the [[p-value]] and rejecting the null hypothesis if <math>p < \alpha</math>.

== Confidence interval ==
The [[confidence interval]] for the difference between two proportions, based on the definitions above, is:<ref name ="Kiernan2014" /><ref name="Su2024" />{{rp|10.6.3}}<math display="block">(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}},</math>where <math>z_{\alpha/2}</math> is the critical value of the standard normal distribution (e.g., 1.96 for a 95% confidence level).

This interval provides a range of plausible values for the true difference between population proportions.

Notice how the variance estimation is different between the hypothesis testing and the confidence intervals. The first uses a pooled variance (based on the null hypothesis), while the second has to estimate the variance using each sample separately (so as to allow for the confidence interval to accommodate a range of differences in proportions). This difference may lead to slightly different results if using the confidence interval as an alternative to the hypothesis testing method.

== Sample size determination and Minimum detectable effect ==
[[Sample size determination]] is the act of choosing the number of observations to include in each group for running the statistical test. For the Two-proportion Z-test, this is closely-related with deciding on the minimum detectable effect.

For finding the required sample size (given some effect size <math>|p_1 - p_2|</math>, power <math>\pi = (1-\beta)</math>, and type I error <math>\alpha</math>), we define that <math>n_1 = \kappa n_2</math>, (when κ = 1, equal sample size is assumed for each group), then:<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Kim HY |title=Statistical notes for clinical researchers: Sample size calculation 2. Comparison of two independent proportions |journal=Restor Dent Endod |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=154–6 |date=May 2016 |pmid=27200285 |pmc=4868880 |doi=10.5395/rde.2016.41.2.154 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Wang |first1=H. |last2=Chow |first2=S.-C. |chapter=Sample Size Calculation for Comparing Proportions |title=Wiley Encyclopedia of Clinical Trials |date=2008 |isbn=978-1-78034-239-9 }}</ref>

<math>
n_2 = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2}{(p_1 - p_2)^2} \times \left( \frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{\kappa} + p_2(1-p_2) \right)^2
</math>

The '''minimum detectable effect''' or '''MDE''' is the smallest difference between two proportions (<math>p_1</math> and <math>p_2</math>) that a statistical test can detect for a chosen [[type I error]] level (<math>\alpha</math>), [[statistical power]] (<math>1-\beta</math>), and sample sizes (<math>n_1</math> and <math>n_2</math>). It is commonly used in study design to determine whether the sample sizes allows for a test with sufficient sensitivity to detect meaningful differences.

The MDE for when using the (two-sided) z-test formula for comparing two proportions, incorporating critical values for <math>\alpha</math> and <math>1-\beta</math>, and the standard errors of the proportions:<ref>COOLSerdash (https://stats.stackexchange.com/users/21054/coolserdash), Two proportion sample size calculation, URL (version: 2023-04-14): https://stats.stackexchange.com/q/612894</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Chow |first1=S-C |last2=Shao |first2=J |last3=Wang |first3=H |last4=Lokhnygina |first4=Y |title=Sample size calculations in clinical research |publisher=CRC Press |edition=3rd |date=2018 |isbn=978-1-351-72712-9 |url={{GBurl|BjkPEAAAQBAJ|pg=PR5}} |series=CRC Biostatistics}}</ref><math display="block">
\text{MDE} = |p_1 - p_2| = z_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)} + z_{1-\beta} \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}},
</math>where <math>z_{1-\alpha/2}</math> is critical value for the significance level, <math>z_{1-\beta}</math> is quantile for the desired power, and <math>p_0=p_1=p_2</math> is when assuming the null is correct.

The MDE depends on the sample sizes, baseline proportions (<math>p_1, p_2</math>), and test parameters. When the baseline proportions are not known, they need to be assumed or roughly estimated from a small study. Larger samples or smaller power requirements leads to a smaller MDE, making the test more sensitive to smaller differences. Researchers may use the MDE to assess the feasibility of detecting meaningful differences before conducting a study.
{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=[Proof]}}

The '''Minimal Detectable Effect (MDE)''' is the smallest difference, denoted as <math>\Delta = |p_1 - p_2|</math>, that satisfies two essential criteria in hypothesis testing:

# The null hypothesis (<math>H_0: p_1 = p_2</math>) is rejected at the specified significance level (<math>\alpha</math>).
# Statistical power (<math>1 - \beta</math>) is achieved under the alternative hypothesis (<math>H_a: p_1 \neq p_2</math>).

Given that the distribution is normal under the null and the alternative hypothesis, for the two criteria to happen, it is required that the distance of <math>|p_1 - p_2|</math> will be such that the critical value for rejecting the null (<math>X_\text{critical}</math>) is exactly in the location in which the probability of exceeding this value, under the null, is (<math>\alpha</math>), and also that the probability of exceeding this value, under the alternative, is <math>1 - \beta</math>.

The first criterion establishes the critical value required to reject the null hypothesis. The second criterion specifies how far the alternative distribution must be from <math>X_\text{critical}</math> to ensure that the probability of exceeding it under the alternative hypothesis is at least <math>1 - \beta</math>.<ref>[https://blog.statsig.com/calculating-sample-sizes-for-a-b-tests-7854d56c2646 Calculating Sample Sizes for A/B Tests]</ref><ref>[https://blog.x.com/engineering/en_us/a/2016/power-minimal-detectable-effect-and-bucket-size-estimation-in-ab-tests Power, minimal detectable effect, and bucket size estimation in A/B tests] (has some nice figures to illustrate the tradeoffs)</ref>

'''Condition 1: Rejecting <math>H_0</math>'''

Under the null hypothesis, the test statistic is based on the pooled standard error (<math>\text{SE}_\text{null}</math>):
<math>
Z_\text{test} = \frac{|p_1 - p_2|}{\text{SE}_\text{null}}, \quad \text{where } \text{SE}_\text{null} = \sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.
</math>

<math>p_0</math> might be estimated (as described above).

To reject <math>H_0</math>, the observed difference must exceed the critical threshold (<math>Z_\text{critical} = z_{\alpha /2 } </math>) after properly inflating it to the SE:
<math>
|p_1 - p_2| \geq X_{critical} = z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}_\text{null}
</math>

If the MDE is defined solely as <math>MDE = z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}_\text{null}</math>, the statistical power would be only 50% because the alternative distribution is symmetric about the threshold. To achieve a higher power level, an additional component is required in the MDE calculation.

'''Condition 2: Achieving power <math>1 - \beta</math>'''

Under the alternative hypothesis, the standard error is (<math>\text{SE}_\text{alt} = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}</math>).
It means that if the alternative distribution was centered around some value (e.g., <math>X_\text{critical}</math>), then the minimal <math>|p_1 - p_2|</math> must be at least larger than <math>z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}_\text{null}</math> to ensure that the probability of detecting the difference under the alternative hypothesis is at least <math>1 - \beta</math>.

'''Combining conditions'''

To meet both conditions, the total detectable difference incorporates components from both the null and alternative distributions. The MDE is defined as:
<math>
\text{MDE} = z_{1- \alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}_\text{null} + z_{1- \beta} \cdot \text{SE}_\text{alt}.
</math>

By summing the critical thresholds from the null and adding to it the relevant quantile from the alternative distributions, the MDE ensures the test satisfies the dual requirements of rejecting <math>H_0</math> at significance level <math>\alpha</math> and achieving statistical power of at least <math>1 - \beta</math>.

{{hidden end}}

== Assumptions and conditions ==
To ensure valid results, the following assumptions must be met:
# Independent random samples: The samples must be drawn independently from the populations of interest.
# Large sample sizes: Typically, <math>n_1+n_2</math> should exceed 20.<ref name="VanVoorhis2007" />{{rp|48}}
# Success or failure condition:<ref>Course notes for [https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/lesson/9/9.1 STAT 200: Elementary Statistics. 9.1 - Two Independent Proportions], Penn State's Department of Statistics</ref><ref name="Su2024" />{{rp|10.6.1}}
## <math>n_1 \hat{p}_1 > 10</math> and <math>n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) > 10</math>
## <math>n_2 \hat{p}_2 > 10</math> and <math>n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) > 10</math>

The z-test is most reliable when sample sizes are large, and all assumptions are satisfied.

== Relation to other statistical methods ==
=== Related tests ===
Using the z-test for hypothesis testing ([[Score test]]) would give the same results as [[Pearson's chi-squared test#Two-by-two contingency tables|Pearson's chi-squared test for a two-by-two contingency table]].<ref>{{cite book |chapter=Confidence Intervals for the Difference Between Two Proportions |chapter-url=https://www.ncss.com/wp-content/themes/ncss/pdf/Procedures/PASS/Confidence_Intervals_for_the_Difference_Between_Two_Proportions.pdf |title=PASS Sample Size Software |publisher=NCSS.com |url=https://www.ncss.com/software/pass/procedures/}}</ref>{{rp|216–7}}<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Newcombe RG |title=Interval estimation for the difference between independent proportions: comparison of eleven methods |journal=Stat Med |volume=17 |issue=8 |pages=873–90 |date=April 1998 |pmid=9595617 |doi=10.1002/(sici)1097-0258(19980430)17:8<873::aid-sim779>3.0.co;2-i }}</ref>{{rp|875}} [[Fisher's exact test]] is more suitable for when the sample sizes are small.

Treatment of 2-by-2 [[contingency table]] has been investigated as early as the 19th century,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Stigler |first=Stephen M. |title=The missing early history of contingency tables |journal=Annales de la Faculté des Sciences de Toulouse: Mathématiques |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=563–573 |year=2002 |doi=10.5802/afst.1039 |doi-broken-date=15 October 2025 |url=http://eudml.org/doc/73594}}
</ref> with further work during the 20th century.<ref>{{cite web |last=Hitchcock |first=David B. |title=Yates and contingency tables: 75 years later |url=https://people.stat.sc.edu/hitchcock/yates75tech.pdf
 |publisher=Electronic Journal for History of Probability & Statistics |year=2009}}</ref>

Notice that:
* When one or more cell counts are small (e.g. below 5<ref name="VanVoorhis2007">{{cite journal |last=VanVoorhis |first=C.R. Wilson |first2=Betsy L. |last2=Morgan |title=Understanding power and rules of thumb for determining sample sizes |journal=Tutorials in quantitative methods for psychology |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=43–50 |date=2007 |doi=10.20982/tqmp.03.2.p043 |url=https://www.tqmp.org/RegularArticles/vol03-2/p043/p043.pdf}}</ref>{{rp|48}}), prefer exact tests (e.g., [[Fisher's exact test]]) or exact confidence intervals.
* For paired or matched binary data use [[McNemar's test]] rather than the two-sample z-test.  
* The choice between pooled and unpooled variance matters: pooled variance is appropriate for hypothesis testing of equality (<math>H_0: p_1=p_2</math>), whereas the unpooled variance is used for confidence intervals.  
* [[Multiple comparisons problem|Multiple testing]], selection effects, and nonrandom sampling can invalidate p-values and CIs; these design issues should be addressed in the study methods.

In [[Bayesian inference]] context, proportions can be modeled using the [[Beta distribution#Bayesian inference|Beta distribution]]. The parallel to two proportion z-test is performing similar inference using the difference of two Beta distributions.<ref>Chen, Y., & Luo, S. (2011). A few remarks on 'Statistical distribution of the difference of two proportions' by Nadarajah and Kotz, Statistics in Medicine 2007; 26 (18): 3518-3523. Statistics in Medicine, 30(15), 1913-1915.</ref>

=== Newcombe's method ===
The standard asymptotic confidence interval (Wald interval) for the difference between proportions can suffer from poor [[Coverage probability|coverage probabilities]], particularly when the sample sizes are small or the proportions are close to 0 or 1. Additionally, the Wald method can sometimes produce "overshoot" limits that extend beyond the meaningful [−1, 1] range.<ref name="Newcombe1998">{{cite journal |last=Newcombe |first=Robert G. |title=Interval estimation for the difference between independent proportions: comparison of eleven methods |journal=Statistics in Medicine |volume=17 |issue=8 |pages=873–890 |date=April 1998 |pmid=9595617 |doi=10.1002/(sici)1097-0258(19980430)17:8<873::aid-sim779>3.0.co;2-i }}</ref> To address this, Robert G. Newcombe proposed a highly robust alternative method based on the [[Binomial proportion confidence interval#Wilson score interval|Wilson score interval]].

Newcombe's method computes the confidence interval for the difference <math>p_1 - p_2</math> by first calculating these individual score intervals for each sample proportion independently. Let <math>(l_1, u_1)</math> be the lower and upper bounds for <math>p_1</math>, and <math>(l_2, u_2)</math> be the lower and upper bounds for <math>p_2</math>. The interval bounds for a given sample proportion <math>\hat{p}</math> with sample size <math>n</math> are calculated as:
<math display="block">\frac{\hat{p} + \frac{z^2}{2n} \pm z \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n} + \frac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \frac{z^2}{n}}</math>
where <math>z</math> is the critical value from the standard normal distribution (e.g., 1.96 for a 95% confidence level).

Once the individual bounds are calculated, the lower limit <math>L</math> and upper limit <math>U</math> for the difference between the two proportions are constructed as follows:<ref name="Newcombe1998" />
<math display="block">L = (\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) - \sqrt{(\hat{p}_1 - l_1)^2 + (u_2 - \hat{p}_2)^2}</math>
<math display="block">U = (\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) + \sqrt{(u_1 - \hat{p}_1)^2 + (\hat{p}_2 - l_2)^2}</math>

This method is frequently recommended over the traditional Wald method because its resulting interval is strictly bounded between −1 and 1, and it aligns much more closely with the nominal confidence level without requiring a [[Yates's correction for continuity|continuity correction]].<ref name="Newcombe1998" /><ref name="Fagerland2015">{{cite journal |last1=Fagerland |first1=Morten W. |last2=Lydersen |first2=Stian |last3=Laake |first3=Petter |title=Recommended confidence intervals for two independent binomial proportions |journal=Statistical Methods in Medical Research |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=224–254 |year=2015 |doi=10.1177/0962280211415469 |pmid=21996567}}</ref>

== Example ==

Suppose group 1 has 120 successes out of 1000 trials (<math>\hat{p}_1=0.12</math>) and group 2 has 150 successes out of 1000 trials (<math>\hat{p}_2=0.15</math>). The pooled proportion is <math>\hat{p}=(120+150)/(1000+1000)=0.135</math>. The pooled standard error is<math display="block">\text{SE}_\text{pooled}=\sqrt{0.135\times0.865\times\left(\dfrac{1}{1000}+\dfrac{1}{1000}\right)}\approx 0.01529.</math>

The z-statistic is<math display="block">z=\dfrac{0.12-0.15}{0.01529}\approx -1.96,</math>giving a two-sided p-value of about 0.0497 (just under 0.05). An approximate 95% confidence interval for the difference using the unpooled standard error is<math display="block">(0.12-0.15)\pm 1.96\sqrt{\dfrac{0.12\times0.88}{1000}+\dfrac{0.15\times0.85}{1000}} \approx (-0.0599,\ -0.0001).</math>Because the 95% CI (just barely) excludes 0 and the p-value is ≈0.0497, the difference is statistically significant at the 5% level by the usual large-sample criteria (but is borderline; conclusions should account for study context and multiple testing if applicable).

== Software implementation ==

Implementations are available in many statistical environments. See below for implementation details in some popular languages. Other implementations also exists for SPSS,<ref>[https://www.spss-tutorials.com/z-test-2-independent-proportions/ Z-Test for 2 Independent Proportions – Quick Tutorial]</ref> SAS,<ref>[https://support.sas.com/kb/22/561.html Usage Note 22561: Testing the equality of two or more proportions from independent samples]</ref> and Minitab.<ref name ="Kiernan2014" />

=== R ===
Use <code>prop.test()</code> with continuity correction disabled:
<syntaxhighlight lang="r">
prop.test(x = c(120, 150), n = c(1000, 1000), correct = FALSE)
</syntaxhighlight>
Output includes z-test equivalent results: chi-squared statistic, p-value, and confidence interval:

<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
	2-sample test for equality of proportions without continuity correction

data:  c(120, 150) out of c(1000, 1000)
X-squared = 3.8536, df = 1, p-value = 0.04964
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -5.992397e-02 -7.602882e-05
sample estimates:
prop 1 prop 2 
  0.12   0.15 
</syntaxhighlight>

=== Python ===
Use <code>proportions_ztest</code> from statsmodels:<ref>[https://www.statsmodels.org/dev/generated/statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportions_ztest.html statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportions_ztest]</ref>
<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest
z, p = proportions_ztest([120, 150], [1000, 1000], 0)
# For CI: from statsmodels.stats.proportion import test_proportions_2indep
</syntaxhighlight>

=== SQL ===
Direct implementation of the formulas from above, using [[Presto (SQL query engine)|Presto]] flavour of SQL (relying on VALUES,<ref>[https://prestodb.io/docs/current/sql/values.html# Presto 0.295 Documentation - VALUES]</ref> inverse_normal_cdf,<ref>[https://prestodb.io/docs/current/functions/math.html#probability-functions-inverse-cdf Mathematical Functions and Operators - Probability Functions: inverse_cdf]</ref> and normal_cdf<ref>[https://prestodb.io/docs/current/functions/math.html#probability-functions-cdf Mathematical Functions and Operators - Probability Functions: cdf]</ref>)

<syntaxhighlight lang="sql">
WITH input_data AS (
  SELECT *, ((n_1 * p_1 + n_2 * p_2) / (n_1 + n_2)) AS p_pooled
  FROM (
    VALUES
      (1000, 1000, 0.12, 0.15)
  ) AS t (n_1, n_2, p_1, p_2)
),
stats_computed AS (
  SELECT
    n_1, n_2, p_1, p_2,
    p_2 - p_1 AS p2_minus_p1,
    SQRT(
      (p_1 * (1 - p_1) / n_1) +
      (p_2 * (1 - p_2) / n_2)
    ) AS se_p2_minus_p1,
    SQRT( p_pooled * (1 -  p_pooled) * (1.0 / n_1 + 1.0 / n_2) ) AS pooled_se,
    inverse_normal_cdf(0, 1, 0.975) AS z_975  -- for 95% CI (1.96)
  FROM input_data
)
SELECT
  n_1,
  n_2,
  ROUND(p_1, 3) AS p_1,
  ROUND(p_2, 3) AS p_2,
  ROUND(p2_minus_p1, 3) AS p2_minus_p1,
  ROUND(se_p2_minus_p1, 3) AS se_p2_minus_p1,
  ROUND(p2_minus_p1 - z_975 * se_p2_minus_p1, 3) AS p2_minus_p1_ci_lower,
  ROUND(p2_minus_p1 + z_975 * se_p2_minus_p1, 3) AS p2_minus_p1_ci_upper,
  ROUND(2 * (1 - normal_cdf(0, 1, ABS(p2_minus_p1)/pooled_se )), 3) AS p_value
FROM stats_computed;
</syntaxhighlight>
